newsitem.title: USA: US sweetener users urge higher sugar import quota.
newsitem.headline: US sweetener users urge higher sugar import quota.

text.p: U.S. sweetener users and cane refiners on Thursday urged the Clinton administration to allow foreign sugar suppliers more access to the U.S. market.

At a seminar on the operation of the U.S tariff-rate quota for sugar, the groups requested that a key trigger level used to determine the annual quota be raised to allow imports to fill a greater portion of domestic demand.
The groups also urged that more of the annual sugar quota be allocated early in the quota year to give importers and suppliers more time to arrange shipments.
For the 1997 quota year, which ends Sep 30, USDA used a 15.5 percent "stocks-to-use ratio" to determine the size of the annual quota, which was initially set at 2.3 million tonnes.
However, using a procedure established in advance, the quota was reduced to 2.1 million tonnes in January, when the projected stocks-to-use ratio rose above 15.5 percent.
The stocks-to-use ratio compares sugar stocks on hand at the end of the quota year to annual consumption. A low ratio reflects tight domestic supplies.
In a recommendation sure to be opposed by sugar growers, the sweetener users and cane refiners urged that the stocks-to-use ratio trigger be raised to at least 16.5 percent.

"We believe the stocks-to-use ratio could up as high as 17 percent without the department facing even a risk of (potentially costly sugar program loan) forfeitures," said Margaret Blamberg, vice-president of economic research and government relations for Domino Sugar Corp.
The United States has had some form of a sugar import quota since 1982 to support domestic sugar prices.
However, inevitable tension between sugar growers and sugar users often led to significant changes in the quota within the course of the year.
To make the quota program more predictable, USDA implement a new system last year.
Using a 15.5 percent stocks-to-use ratio as a goal, it tentatively set the quota at 2.3 million tonnes.

It initially allocated only 1.7 million tonnes and left the remaining 600,000 to be allocated in batches of 200,000 each in January, March and May -- assuming the projected stocks-to-use ratio remained below the trigger level.
In January, the projected ratio rose above 15.5 percent, which led to the cancellation of that's month allocation.

That, in turn, had the effect of tightening domestic supplies so the projected stocks-to-use ratio remained below 15.5 percent in March and May and allocations for those months went ahead as scheduled.

There was universal agreement at the meeting sponsored by the Sweeteners Users Association and United States Cane Sugar Refiners' Association that USDA's new system for administering the sugar improvement was a big improvement over the past.
But USDA should continue to fine tune the program to make it more market-oriented, industry representatives urged.

In addition to raising the stocks-to-use trigger, USDA should allocate 90 percent of the quota intially -- instead of 70 percent -- and release further allocations in November, January and March, rather than Janaury, March and May, Blamberg said.

Wes McAden, representing the C and H Sugar Co, also urged the country allocations under the quota be "realigned" to recognize that the West Coast is increasingly dependent on imports because of the decline in Hawaiian production over the past several years.

Lee McConnell, director of commodities for Bloomer Chocalate, estimated that a 16.5 percent stocks-to-use trigger would result in a 1998 quota of 2.3 million tonnes, based on current supply and demand conditions.

Don Westfall, vice president of Promar International, a business consulting firm, using different set of calculations, said USDA could set the 1998 quota at about 2.2 million tonnes, without the fear of loan forfeitures.

Before the 1996 farm bill, USDA was required by law to operate the sugar program to avoid forfeitures. That meant it had to use the quota to keep U.S. sugar prices above the sugar cane price support loan rate of 18 cents per pound.
USDA is no longer required to run the sugar program at no cost, but "it doesn't make a lot of sense" to set the quota so high that it triggers forfeitures, said Steve Hammond, USDA sugar team leader.

Still, when Hammond was asked if there was enough of a gap between market prices and the USDA loan rate to raise the stocks-to-use trigger without the risk of forfeitures, he pointed to price chart that suggested there was.
"I'll let you answer your question," he told reporters, declining to comment further on that point.
While many of the comments made by the sweetener users and refiners make sense, sugar growers will likely push for a more restrictive import policy, Hammond said.
USDA will consider all views before making its final decision on the 1998 quota. That could come as early as late August, but the formal deadline is September 17, he said.
(-- Doug Palmer, 202 898 8341)
